articles.title: MSC raises December FAK rates to Mediterranean and Black Sea
articles.summary: MSC has announced higher Freight All Kinds (FAK) rates for shipments from the Far East to the Mediterranean, North Africa and the Black Sea, effective from 1 December 2026, while maintaining its existing rates to Northern Europe. articles.body: MSC has announced higher Freight All Kinds (FAK) rates for shipments from the Far East to the Mediterranean, North Africa and the Black Sea, effective from 1 December 2026, while maintaining its existing rates to Northern Europe. The new tariffs will remain in effect until further notice, but no later than 14 December 2026. They cover shipments from all Far East ports, including Japan, South Korea and Southeast Asia, to destinations across Northern Europe, the Western and Eastern Mediterranean, the Adriatic, North Africa and the Black Sea. Compared with the carrier’s rates for the second half of November, the new tariffs represent increases across most destinations. For 40-foot dry and high-cube containers, rates to the Western Mediterranean and Adriatic will rise by US$1,200 to US$6,500, while those to the Eastern Mediterranean will increase by US$800 to the same level. Black Sea rates will also increase by US$800, reaching US$6,700 per 40-foot container. Northern European rates will remain unchanged at US$4,600. New MSC freight rates from 1 December The announced FAK rates, expressed in US dollars, are as follows: Destination 20-foot dry 40-foot dry/HC North Europe 3,220 4,600 West Mediterranean 5,100 6,500 Adriatic 5,100 6,500 East Mediterranean 5,100 6,500 Black Sea 5,200 6,700 Algeria 6,100 8,200 Libya 6,000 8,000 Morocco (Casablanca) 5,500 7,000 Tunisia 6,000 8,000 North African destinations will continue to carry the highest published rates. Algeria will reach US$8,200 per 40-foot container, an increase of US$600 from the second half of November, while rates to Libya and Tunisia will each rise by US$800 to US$8,000. Morocco’s Casablanca rate will also increase by US$800, reaching US$7,000 per 40-foot container. Additional surcharges and conditions MSC stated that the announced rates apply from base port to base port, with shipments involving out-ports subject to the usual Transport Additional Origin and Destination (TAO/TAD) charges. The published FAK rates already include the ocean freight component and a Global Fuel Surcharge (GFS) of US$304 per TEU for December, compared with US$266 per TEU in November. They also incorporate an Emission Control Area (ECA) surcharge of US$15 per TEU for Mediterranean destinations and specified Northern European countries, or US$52 per TEU for other Nordic and Baltic destinations. Additional charges include a Carbon Limitation Surcharge (CLS) of US$20 per TEU and a Carbon Review Surcharge (CRS) of US$90 per TEU for Northern Europe and US$133 per TEU for the Mediterranean. Piracy Risk Surcharge (PRS) and Suez Canal Surcharge (SCS) provisions also apply according to MSC’s separate announcement dated 4 November 2026. The carrier noted that its FAK rates exclude IMO-classified commodities and high-value cargo. Terminal handling charges and other applicable costs may also be added. The announced figures represent MSC’s published tariffs for the specified period rather than confirmed transaction rates paid by shippers.

articles.title: Konecranes secures mobile harbor crane order for Peru’s Port of Matarani
articles.summary: Konecranes has received an order from Terminal Internacional del Sur (Tisur) for a new mobile harbor crane at the Port of Matarani in southern Peru. The order marks the company’s first sale of a factory-new mobile harbor crane in Peru. The agreement covers one Konecranes Gottwald ESP.6 Mobile Harbor Crane. It was...
articles.body: Konecranes has received an order from Terminal Internacional del Sur (Tisur) for a new mobile harbor crane at the Port of Matarani in southern Peru. The order marks the company’s first sale of a factory-new mobile harbor crane in Peru. The agreement covers one Konecranes Gottwald ESP.6 Mobile Harbor Crane. It was recorded in the third quarter of 2026, while the equipment is expected to enter operation by the end of March 2027. The investment forms part of Tisur’s US$598 million port modernisation programme. The new crane will handle containers, general cargo and project cargo at the multipurpose terminal. It will have a maximum lifting capacity of 125 tonnes. Tisur already operates a pre-owned Konecranes Gottwald crane manufactured in the 1990s. The operator’s experience with this equipment played a role in its decision to purchase the new model. “Our existing crane has proven its reliability over many years. We wanted to build on that experience with a new, high-performance crane to support our ambitious plans for the port. The excellent advice and strong local service support from Konecranes were also key factors in our decision,” said Mauricio Nuñez del Prado, General Manager, Tisur. Hybrid technology supports port operations The new crane will use a hybrid drive system with capacitors to reduce energy consumption and emissions. Its design will also allow a future conversion to fully electric operation. In addition, Tisur has selected a motor grab for bulk cargo handling. This will allow the crane to support different types of cargo at the terminal. “We’re delighted to break new ground in Peru together with Tisur. Our relationship with them demonstrates the value of working closely with customers over the long term, supported by reliable equipment and a strong local service network,” said Alfredo Canibano, Regional Sales Manager, Konecranes Port Solutions. The order adds new cargo-handling equipment to the Port of Matarani as Tisur continues its wider modernisation programme.

articles.title: Small Modular Reactors for Maritime Shipping: A Nuclear Propulsion Pathway
articles.summary: Nuclear power has already crossed oceans. The harder question is whether modern small modular reactors can be integrated, licensed and financed for merchant ships, and where they make sense first.In 2023 the International Maritime Organization…
articles.body: Small Modular Reactors for Maritime Shipping: A Nuclear Propulsion Pathway Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. By Lakshya, Krish Uniyal and Raj Singh | International Maritime Institute, Greater Noida, India November 12, 2026 Conceptual view of an SMR module, turbo-electric conversion and reinforced containment zone installed in a bulk carrier. Credit: Authors (Lakshya, Krish Uniyal, Raj Singh) About the Author: Lakshya is a third-year B.Tech Marine Engineering student at IMI Noida, researching small modular reactor propulsion, sustainable shipping, AI-driven hull health assessment and predictive maintenance. About the Author: Krish Uniyal, third-year B.Tech Marine Engineering student at IMI Noida, researches maritime decarbonization and advanced propulsion, specializing in commercial nuclear shipping economics and Gen-IV reactors. About the Author: Raj Singh, a third-year B.Tech Marine Engineering student at IMI Greater Noida, researching Small Modular Reactor (SMR)-based nuclear propulsion for sustainable maritime shipping and decarbonization. Nuclear power has already crossed oceans. The harder question is whether modern small modular reactors can be integrated, licensed and financed for merchant ships, and where they make sense first. In 2023 the International Maritime Organization (IMO) set a goal of net-zero greenhouse gas emissions from international shipping by around 2050. LNG, methanol, ammonia and hydrogen each solve part of the problem and create another. Nuclear propulsion offers a different trade: fuel so energy-dense that a ship can sail for years without bunkering, with no combustion emissions at the point of use. Nuclear ships are not new. Four civil vessels proved the concept decades ago. What is new is the Small Modular Reactor (SMR), and the fact that classification societies are now approving ship designs built around it. Our study asks whether SMR propulsion is a realistic option for merchant shipping. The short answer: promising for selected high-utilization ships, but not a universal replacement, and the barriers are as much institutional as technical. More than a reactor A nuclear ship takes its thrust from heat released by fission. In a pressurized water reactor (PWR), the coolant is held at high pressure so it does not boil while carrying heat from the fuel. But a marine installation is far more than a reactor and a steam generator. As Fig. 1 shows, heat passes through a steam cycle or intermediate heat exchanger to a turbine-generator, then through a high-voltage switchboard to the propulsion motors, with waste heat rejected to the sea. Electric transmission gives designers freedom, including multiple shafts and flexible power allocation, but it adds conversion equipment and demands redundancy against correlated failures. One point is easy to miss: what matters is net propulsion power, not the reactor's thermal rating. Emergency systems, pumps, ventilation, hotel loads and low-power operation all take their share. Large container ships, tankers and bulkers need tens to hundreds of megawatts, which may mean several modules, and reliability must then be judged for the whole ship rather than reactor by reactor. SMR propulsion chain, from reactor module to propeller, with shielding, emergency decay-heat removal and cooling supporting the plant. Credit: Authors (Lakshya, Krish Uniyal, Raj Singh) Proof from the first nuclear merchant ships Four civil ships supply the real-world evidence. The US-built NS Savannah, with a 74–76 MW thermal PWR and about 16.4 MW at the shaft, logged roughly 450,000 nautical miles on a single refueling. Germany's Otto Hahn, with an integrated 38 MW reactor, covered around 650,000. Japan's Mutsu (36 MW) developed automatic load-following and showed stable response in 1991 sea trials. The Soviet icebreaker Lenin, commissioned in 1959, began with three reactors totalling 270 MW thermal and was later upgraded to about 342 MW. Together they show that turning nuclear heat into ship propulsion works. They also carry a warning: Savannah's retirement showed that technical success does not guarantee commercial viability. Which reactor? PWRs have the strongest marine record, but a reactor in a protected central hull section competes with cargo space. Advanced concepts promise more. Molten salt reactors (MSRs) run hot at low pressure, though corrosion and chemistry questions remain open. Lead-cooled fast reactors (LFRs) use low-pressure heavy-metal coolant but bring fuel-cycle and safeguards complexity. Heat-pipe microreactors are passive and compact, but their limited output suits smaller vessels and auxiliary roles. High-temperature gas-cooled reactors still need validation at merchant-ship scale. Fig. 2 shows the trade: advanced designs offer long refueling intervals, yet only the PWR is close to commercial maturity. The Nuclear Mother-Daughter Transshipment Network (N-MDTN), the authors' proposed concept: nuclear systems stay on the trunk route while non-nuclear feeders serve restricted regional ports. Credit: Authors (Lakshya, Krish Uniyal, Raj Singh) Our central proposal tackles the most awkward problem: every port a nuclear ship visits must accept it. The Nuclear Mother-Daughter Transshipment Network (N-MDTN) sidesteps this. A nuclear-powered mother vessel sails long-haul trunk voyages between a few nuclear-enabled gateway ports, while conventional daughter vessels carry cargo onward to regional ports that never need nuclear acceptance.The logic mirrors existing mother-daughter distribution systems, but it concentrates reactors, specialized crews, regulatory responsibility and emergency capability in one trunk service. That shrinks the number of ports needing nuclear-specific preparedness and allows nuclear corridors to be introduced in phases. Strict separation is the design rule. Daughter vessels handle cargo only, with no reactor fuel, coolant, radioactive waste or access to nuclear machinery. Gateway terminals act as controlled zones with segregated cargo operations, mooring safeguards, weather limits and emergency separation procedures. Safety cases must show that no transfer operation or feeder incident can compromise reactor shutdown, decay-heat removal, containment or emergency power. N-MDTN remains a prospective model, and moving energy between vessels would add significant technical requirements. Technology readiness level and refueling interval of candidate marine reactors (also embedded in the manuscript). Credit: Authors' comparative assessment Safety and security at sea Ships add hazards that land plants never face: collision, grounding, flooding, fire and blackout. Decay heat continues after shutdown, so the seawater cooling interface must fail safe. The marine-specific danger is common-cause failure, where redundant systems sharing a compartment, cable run or sea intake fail together, so physical and functional separation is essential. Passive cooling helps, but passive features alone do not guarantee accident tolerance. Security is a separate discipline from safety. It means protecting reactor, material and control systems against theft and sabotage through layered physical protection, controlled access, cybersecurity and coordination with flag, coastal and port authorities. Crews need combined nuclear and maritime competence, built on simulator-based training. Regulation is the real bottleneck Nuclear ships must satisfy maritime law and nuclear regulation at once. SOLAS Chapter VIII and the IMO's 1981 Code of Safety for Nuclear Merchant Ships remain the operative international benchmark. In June 2025 the IMO's Maritime Safety Committee tasked its Ship Design and Construction sub-committee with revising the Code in a technology-neutral way, drawing on IAEA standards. A work plan was agreed in January 2026, with adoption targeted for 2030 (a date that may change), so the updated framework is not yet mandatory. Flag states need the capacity to license a nuclear installation, and registration does not guarantee entry to foreign ports. Classification societies must bridge marine and nuclear standards, and liability and insurance need provisions that conventional policies lack. International harmonization is a prerequisite for deployment, not a current condition. Industry and governments are moving Design work is accelerating. In October 2025 DNV granted HD KSOE an Approval in Principle (AiP) for a 15,000 TEU SMR-powered container ship designed for 24 knots. ABS and HD Hyundai agreed in March 2026 to design a 16,000 TEU ship with nuclear-linked electric propulsion. Lloyd's Register granted an AiP on June 2 for a 7,000 CEU car carrier using a molten salt reactor, and ABS followed in July with an AiP for a 15,000 TEU ship with two such reactors. An AiP is a preliminary independent assessment, not a nuclear license, an operating certificate or proof of commercial viability. Policy is following. In the U.S., the Maritime Administration (MARAD) opened an SMR request for information in May, then signed cooperation agreements with the Port of Long Beach in July and with CORE POWER in August. Days later the International Atomic Energy Agency launched ATLAS, an initiative backed by 26 countries to build licensing and safeguards frameworks for nuclear technology at sea. Economics: utilization decides High energy density does not make nuclear automatically cheaper. Owners must add the reactor, shielding, ship integration, licensing, training and maintenance. The test is whether extra capital cost is repaid by discounted fuel savings, avoided carbon costs and operating advantages, after nuclear operating expenses and financing risk premiums. The best cases combine long annual operating hours, long service lives, steady propulsion demand and stable routes. A Reactor-as-a-Service (RaaS) model could ease the burden. A specialist provider would own the reactor and fuel and handle refueling, servicing and spent fuel, while the shipowner keeps the hull and conventional systems, paying a fixed availability fee plus a per-MWh tariff. Nuclear liability, however, is set by statute and cannot be transferred by contract alone. Fuel supply matters too: low-enriched and high-assay low-enriched uranium need dependable, regulated supply chains. Where nuclear fits first Large container ships, tankers, ice-class cargo ships and offshore support vessels with continuous power demand show the strongest cases. Low-utilization bulk carriers and small coastal vessels are weaker, and passenger ships raise public-acceptance questions. For India, with its nuclear infrastructure and large shipping sector, the opportunity is strategic, but nuclear-grade manufacturing and quality assurance would take sustained effort. Outlook Nuclear propulsion shifts environmental risk rather than removing it: operational emissions largely disappear, but fuel-cycle emissions, radioactive waste and decommissioning remain. SMR propulsion is therefore best treated as a targeted option for future fleets, not an immediate replacement for conventional fuels. The sensible path is phased: demonstration projects, incremental licensing, gradual port acceptance, and reactor qualification that goes beyond land-based testing to cover vibration, shock, collision, grounding, fire and flooding. Commercialization is a system-of-systems problem. Reactors, ship integration, safety, regulation, ports, people, liability and finance must advance together. If they do, SMRs could power a safe, reliable and economically viable part of the future blue economy. References 1. International Maritime Organization (IMO), 2023 Strategy on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships, Res. MEPC.377(80), 2023. 2. IMO, SOLAS 1974 as amended, Chapter VIII; Code of Safety for Nuclear Merchant Ships, Res. A.491(XII), 1981. 3. IMO, SDC 12 meeting summary, Jan. 19-23, 2026 (work plan for revising the Nuclear Code and SOLAS Chapter VIII). 4. International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), Advances in SMR Developments 2024; Technical Reports Series No. 410 (2002), civil nuclear ship data. 5. IAEA, ATLAS launch forum, Washington, Aug. 26-27, 2026; IMO statement on its participation. 6. DNV, "HD KSOE awarded DNV AiP for SMR-powered container vessel design," Oct. 23, 2025; DNV, Maritime Nuclear Propulsion, 2025. 7. ABS and HD Hyundai agreement on a 16,000 TEU nuclear-linked electric propulsion ship, March 2026 (World Nuclear News). 8. Lloyd's Register, "LR backs nuclear car carrier concept at Posidonia," June 2, 2026. 9. articles.title: New ultra-deep oil & gas discovery marks ‘major breakthrough’ in Bohai Sea
articles.summary: CNOOC has revealed an ultra-deep natural gas find in the central Bohai Sea, with a high-yield volcanic well testing at 800,000 cubic meters per day.
articles.body: Exploration & Production November 12, 2026 · 1 minute ago New ultra-deep oil & gas discovery marks ‘major breakthrough’ in Bohai Sea CNOOC has revealed an ultra-deep natural gas find in the central Bohai Sea, with a high-yield volcanic well testing at 800,000 cubic meters per day. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Offshore platform (for illustration purposes) Source: CNOOC Chinese state-owned oil and gas giant China National Offshore Oil Corporation (CNOOC) has made a high-yield natural gas discovery in volcanic rock more than 5,700 meters beneath the central Bohai Sea, opening doors to a new frontier for ultra-deep exploration in the region and bringing the company one step closer to building a trillion-cubic-meter gas province off the coast of China. CNOOC has drilled a high-yield volcanic oil and gas well in ultra-deep formations over 5,000 meters deep in Bohai, said to represent a major breakthrough in ultra-deep natural gas exploration offshore China. The well, which is adjacent to the Bozhong Sag , the largest hydrocarbon-rich sag in Bohai, encountered a cumulative total of over 120 meters of gas pay zone in volcanic formations and was completed at a depth of 5,770 meters. The well was tested to produce approximately 800,000 cubic meters (around 28 million cubic feet) per day of natural gas, uncovering promising exploration prospects in the offshore ultra-deep volcanic rocks and promoting the natural gas exploration process in the Bozhong Sag. " In recent years, CNOOC Limited has continued to strengthen theoretical innovation in deep and ultra-deep oil and gas enrichment in basins with high heat flow and strong activity, and to intensify research on key technologies. Exploration in China’s offshore areas has achieved a major leap from shallow to deep and ultra-deep formations. The success of this well has opened up a new play for offshore ultra-deep natural gas exploration and expanded the scope of deep oil and gas exploration in Bohai. It is of positive significance for accelerating the ultra-deep exploration process in Bohai and for building a major gas province of one trillion cubic meters in Bohai. " — Xu Changgui Chief Scientist and Chief Geologist of China National Offshore Oil Corporation (CNOOC) Related Articles Business & Finance CNOOC’s 2026 run powered by 9 start-ups, 5 new oil & gas discoveries, and 23 appraisals 2 min read While the ultra-deep formations in Bohai are geologically complex, making reservoir prediction difficult, CNOOC has continued to make what it describes as breakthroughs in its theoretical understanding of offshore ultra-deep oil and gas exploration. The company independently developed key offshore deep multi-source broadband three-dimensional (3D) seismic exploration technologies and innovative methods for predicting high-quality reservoirs in ultra-deep buried hills. The Chinese player points out that its efforts enabled it to identify the favorable ultra-deep volcanic natural gas enrichment zones in the Bozhong Sag, discovering a high-yield oil and gas well, and marking significant progress in ultra-deep volcanic natural gas exploration in Bohai. articles.summary: Singapore has retained its position as the world’s leading maritime hub, while Shanghai has climbed to second place and Asia now accounts for three of the world’s five highest-ranked maritime...

Join the leading maritime news network File Photo of Singapore Anchorage: anek.soowannaphoom/Shutterstock Singapore has retained its position as the world’s leading maritime hub, while Shanghai has climbed to second place and Asia now accounts for three of the world’s five highest-ranked maritime cities, according to a new report from DNV and Menon Economics. The Leading Maritime Cities 2026 report, released Thursday, ranks Singapore first overall, followed by Shanghai, London, Rotterdam and Tokyo. Singapore has held the top position since the report was first published in 2015, maintaining its lead through a combination of shipping activity, port infrastructure, maritime services and investment in technology. The biggest shift in this year’s rankings came from Shanghai, which climbed from fourth to second place, overtaking both Rotterdam and London. Tokyo also returned to the top five, replacing Oslo, which ranked fifth in 2024. The results mark a shift toward Asia, which now accounts for three of the top five maritime cities, compared with two in the previous edition. Singapore ranked first in three of the report’s five categories: Shipping, Ports and Logistics, and Attractiveness and Competitiveness. It also placed third in Maritime Finance and Law and fourth in Maritime Technology. Its position reflects the concentration of shipowners and fleet managers operating in the city-state, alongside one of the world’s most important ports, extensive liner shipping connections and growing capabilities in alternative-fuel bunkering. “This has been a year of disruption and adjustment for the maritime industry,” said Cristina Saenz de Santa Maria, CEO Maritime at DNV. “Faced with these challenges, the leading maritime cities have demonstrated that leadership is built not on a single activity, but on breadth.” While Singapore maintained its lead, the report highlights how different maritime centers are competing through their respective strengths. Shanghai’s rise underscores the growing influence of Asian maritime hubs, while London and Rotterdam remain among the world’s leading centers for maritime business, services and port-related activity. North American maritime hubs lost ground in the latest rankings. New York remained the region’s highest-ranked city but slipped from sixth to eighth place globally. Houston fell five positions to 20th, while Los Angeles dropped from 19th to 25th. Vancouver, Canada recorded an even steeper decline, falling from 13th to 28th place. The changes come as Asian maritime centers gain ground in the rankings, although DNV and Menon Economics caution that methodological updates in the 2026 report may affect comparisons with previous editions. The report also points to Dubai as a city to watch. In a survey of maritime industry experts looking ahead five years, Dubai ranked third among the cities expected to lead the global maritime sector. “This year, that points to a shift in the balance of maritime power. Asia now holds three of the top five places, up from two in 2024,” said Erik Jakobsen, partner and chair of Menon Economics. “At the same time, established European hubs such as London and Rotterdam continue to demonstrate the importance of strong maritime services and port-industrial clusters.” The rankings are based on an assessment of 50 maritime cities across five categories: Shipping, Maritime Finance and Law, Maritime Technology, Ports and Logistics, and Attractiveness and Competitiveness. Researchers initially screened more than 15,000 cities using maritime industry data before selecting 50 for a more detailed evaluation. The final assessment uses 48 indicators and incorporates responses from more than 200 maritime industry experts worldwide. Now in its seventh edition, the report has expanded its methodology to account for changes reshaping the maritime industry, including the energy transition, technological development, workforce availability and resilience. DNV and Menon Economics caution that changes in rankings should be viewed in the context of those methodological updates, which can affect comparisons with previous editions. The findings also suggest that maritime competitiveness increasingly depends on more than fleet ownership or cargo volumes alone. “Cities compete from different positions, and their strengths reflect the role they play in the global maritime industry,” said Shahrin Osman, global business development leader for maritime advisory at DNV and co-author of the report. “Those that come out on top link infrastructure, commercial decision-making, specialist services, technology and talent into a single working cluster.” For Singapore, that combination has been enough to keep it at the top of the rankings for more than a decade, even as competition among the world’s leading maritime centers intensifies. articles.title: GEODIS launches new rail freight connection between Italy and France
articles.summary: GEODIS has launched a new rail freight service connecting Vicenza in northern Italy with Noisy-le-Sec, near Paris. The new route expands the company’s European intermodal network and provides another transport option for businesses in Italy’s Veneto region. articles.body: GEODIS has launched a new rail freight service connecting Vicenza in northern Italy with Noisy-le-Sec, near Paris. The new route expands the company’s European intermodal network and provides another transport option for businesses in Italy’s Veneto region. The first train departed on 19 October 2026, marking the start of the service operated by Captrain and Hexafret. Both companies belong to Rail Logistics Europe, part of the SNCF Group alongside GEODIS. Initially, the service offers one departure per week in each direction. However, GEODIS plans to increase the frequency to two weekly departures per direction from January 2027. The connection is designed to transport several types of freight, including packaged liquid and powder goods. It also extends the company’s existing rail services in northern Italy, which already cover Lombardy, Piedmont and Emilia-Romagna through its Novara connection. New service targets intermodal freight growth According to GEODIS, the new rail connection can reduce CO₂ emissions per shipment by an average of 80% compared with diesel-powered road transport. The estimate includes road transport before and after the rail journey, while actual savings depend on operating conditions. The company based its emissions comparison on EcoTransIT World calculations. In addition, the service can carry up to 28 tonnes of goods per transport unit, compared with the 25 tonnes typically transported by road. GEODIS aims to reach an annual volume of 6,500 swap bodies by 2027. The planned increase in service frequency will support this target as the company expands its intermodal transport activities. The company also expects the rail connection to offer greater cost stability compared with road-only transport, particularly during periods of fluctuating fuel prices. “With the Vicenza-Paris connection, we are expanding our intermodal offer and introducing a new railway axis to serve companies in the North East of Italy,” said Marc Vollet, EVP European Road Network, GEODIS. The route strengthens the company’s existing freight network between France and Italy. It also provides businesses in northeastern Italy with a direct rail connection to the Paris region. Captrain and Hexafret will provide rail transport services for the new connection, drawing on their existing European operations. The service enters operation against a backdrop of significant trade flows between the two countries. According to GEODIS, bilateral trade in goods and services reached €136 billion in 2025. Italy ranks as France’s fourth-largest trading partner, while France is Italy’s second-largest. Around 4,000 companies operate across both markets, supporting demand for cross-border freight transport. The latest connection forms part of GEODIS’ wider strategy to expand intermodal services and provide lower-emission alternatives to long-distance road transport.

Join the leading maritime news network Crews prepare to sink the former ocean liner SS United States to create an artificial reef about 22 miles off the coast of Destin, Florida, US, November 11, 2026. Tony Giberson/USA Today Network via REUTERS. The legendary ocean liner, which still holds the transatlantic speed record, took roughly eight hours to sink off Florida’s Gulf Coast, ending a remarkable chapter in American maritime history. The SS United States , the fastest ocean liner ever built and one of the last great symbols of America’s maritime golden age, sank off Florida’s Gulf Coast Wednesday night, November 11, bringing a 74-year journey to an end. The 990-foot vessel disappeared beneath the Gulf shortly after 9 p.m. local time, roughly eight hours after crews began the controlled sinking operation about 22 nautical miles southwest of Destin-Fort Walton Beach. The ship, once celebrated as America’s Flagship, will now begin a new chapter as what officials describe as the world’s largest artificial reef. But the grand old liner did not go down easily. Despite extensive preparations to allow seawater to flood the ship, the sinking took considerably longer than initially anticipated. As darkness fell, the SS United States remained stubbornly afloat, slowly settling deeper into the water. In the final moments, video showed the vessel descending stern-first, with her bow rising sharply as she rolled to port before disappearing beneath the surface. The dramatic finish raised questions about whether the ship settled upright on the seabed as intended. Her final resting position was not immediately confirmed, with underwater inspections expected Thursday. After several hours, the SS United States, an ocean liner, is intentionally sunk off the coast of Florida to become the world's largest artificial reef. pic.twitter.com/DwvU2Njf0f At nearly 1,000 feet long in water approximately 180 feet deep, the ship’s final descent was a complex operation. The stern-first sinking and pronounced port list made it difficult to determine from surface video alone whether the vessel had landed on an even keel. The operation was overseen by Coleen Marine, a contractor specializing in end-of-life vessel services. Unlike sinkings that use explosives to rapidly open a hull, the SS United States was sent down through controlled flooding. Crews had removed hundreds of portholes, cut openings between decks and prepared the vessel’s internal tanks to allow seawater to enter. The approach was intended to produce a controlled descent, but the size and internal structure of the ship made the process challenging. “She’s a big ship,” Okaloosa County spokesperson Nick Tomecek told reporters, acknowledging that the operation took longer than expected. Associated Press reported that the $13.5 million project ultimately concluded Wednesday evening. For generations of mariners and ocean liner enthusiasts, the sinking marked a bittersweet farewell to a vessel that once represented the height of American passenger shipping. The SS United States was the vision of legendary naval architect William Francis Gibbs, who spent much of his career pursuing the dream of building an American ocean liner capable of outperforming Europe’s finest ships. Built by Newport News Shipbuilding in Virginia for United States Lines, the ship entered service in 1952 as a technological marvel. At 990 feet long, she was larger than the RMS Titanic , powered by steam turbines developing approximately 240,000 shaft horsepower, and designed with an extraordinary emphasis on speed, lightweight construction and fire safety. Her design also reflected the strategic realities of the early Cold War. Developed with federal support, the vessel was intended to serve as a luxury passenger liner and, if needed, a high-speed military troop transport. But it was her maiden voyage that secured her place in maritime history. In July 1952, the SS United States crossed the Atlantic in just three days, 10 hours and 40 minutes, averaging 35.59 knots and capturing the coveted Blue Riband from Britain’s RMS Queen Mary . More than seven decades later, her west-to-east transatlantic speed record remains unbroken by an ocean liner. The ship became a national showpiece, carrying presidents, celebrities, business leaders and thousands of ordinary passengers between the United States and Europe. Grace Kelly, Elizabeth Taylor and John F. Kennedy were among her famous passengers. For nearly two decades, her distinctive red, white and blue funnels were an unmistakable presence on the North Atlantic. Despite her extraordinary speed and prestige, the SS United States could not escape the transformation of transatlantic travel. The rise of commercial aviation steadily eroded demand for passenger liners, making it increasingly difficult to justify the enormous cost of operating a ship built for speed. In November 1969, after approximately 800 transatlantic crossings, the SS United States was withdrawn from service. She would never carry paying passengers again. What followed was a succession of ownership changes, failed redevelopment proposals and long periods of inactivity. The ship spent years laid up in Virginia before eventually arriving in Philadelphia in 1996. There, she remained for nearly three decades, her once-proud hull gradually deteriorating along the Delaware River. Although her engines had fallen silent and much of her original interior had been removed, the vessel continued to inspire a passionate preservation movement. The nonprofit SS United States Conservancy, led for years by Susan Gibbs, granddaughter of the ship’s designer, worked to secure a permanent future for the liner. Proposals envisioned converting her into a floating hotel, museum, entertainment complex or waterfront attraction. None ultimately succeeded. As gCaptain reported in June 2024 , a legal battle over pier fees and the ship’s longtime berth brought preservation efforts to a crisis. A federal court ruling requiring the vessel to leave Philadelphia forced her owners to confront an increasingly difficult reality: without a viable redevelopment project or another place to dock, the ship faced the prospect of being scrapped. In October 2024, ownership of the SS United States was transferred to Okaloosa County, Florida, under an agreement to transform the historic liner into an artificial reef. The decision offered an alternative to demolition, but it also meant abandoning the longstanding dream of preserving the entire ship above water. On February 19, 2025, the SS United States departed Philadelphia under tow , passing down the Delaware River and leaving behind the city that had been her home for nearly 30 years. She arrived in Mobile, Alabama, the following month, where contractors began the extensive process of preparing the vessel for deployment. According to Okaloosa County, all 128 fuel and lubricant tanks were emptied and cleaned, environmental remediation was carried out across her 12 decks, and hundreds of historic objects and components were removed for preservation. Among the items saved were the vessel’s iconic funnels, radar mast and other artifacts intended for a future land-based museum dedicated to her history. The project faced a last-minute legal challenge from preservation advocates raising environmental concerns, but an emergency request to halt the sinking was denied. On November 9, the SS United States left Mobile under tow for the last leg of her journey. Unlike her celebrated Atlantic crossings, there were no passengers aboard, no record to chase and no port of arrival. Her destination was the ocean floor. The ship’s sinking on Veterans Day carried an additional historical resonance. Although she was never called upon to serve as a troop transport, her design was closely tied to America’s national defense during the Cold War. Once established on the seabed, the wreck is expected to attract marine life, divers and recreational fishermen, creating a major new attraction along Florida’s Emerald Coast. The project remains controversial among preservation advocates who had hoped the ship could survive as a museum or waterfront landmark. Others see the artificial reef as a more dignified outcome than dismantling her for scrap. Both views reflect the extraordinary attachment the vessel inspired long after she ceased to be commercially useful. The SS United States was built during an era when national prestige could be measured by the speed, size and sophistication of a country’s merchant fleet. She was a product of American shipyards, American engineering and a belief that the nation’s merchant marine could compete with the world’s best. Today, no American-flagged ocean liner makes the regularly scheduled transatlantic crossings that once defined her career. Her sinking marks the physical end of that history above the waterline. But the achievement she represented remains. For 74 years, no ocean liner has surpassed the transatlantic speed record she established on her maiden voyage. The ship that once raced across the Atlantic faster than any ocean liner before or since now rests beneath the Gulf, her days of crossing oceans finally over. The SS United States will never sail again, but her record—and her place in American maritime history—will endure. articles.body: UAV Navigation-Grupo Oesía Launches UAS Heading Estimation System Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 12, 2026 © UAV Navigation-Grupo Oesía © UAV Navigation-Grupo Oesía UAV Navigation-Grupo Oesía, provider of guidance, navigation and control solutions for unmanned vehicles, announced the release of the HES01, a Heading Estimation System providing navigation for unmanned aircraft systems (UAS). The HES01 combines dual GNSS signals with RTK precision, an integrated internal magnetometer and a high-accuracy MEMS-based Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) to achieve sub-centimeter precision landings when paired with VECTOR autopilots (Flight Control Computer, FCC) and the Ground Hub Unit, GHU-100. Additionally, the HES01 is an ideal complement to the company's Visual Navigation System (VNS01) when operating in hostile or contested environments, where precise heading estimation is essential for GNSS-denied navigation. HES01 features include: Up to 0.4º Accurate Heading Estimation: The HES01 provides true heading in both static and dynamic conditions, with no alignment maneuver required. Heading reference for GNSS-denied navigation: Precise heading estimation is essential for GNSS-denied navigation, particularly in demanding applications such as effectors and loitering munitions operating in contested environments, while making the HES01 a key complement for vision-based navigation such as VNS01. RTK-based autonomous recovery on moving decks: The HES01 tracks a landing point that moves with the mothership. RTK corrections provide centimeter-level relative positioning, while the internal IMU compensates for GCS motion, a capability particularly relevant for maritime operations, where it also compensates for the pitch, roll and vertical motion induced by swell. Magnetic heading that holds up under EMI (Electro-Magnetic Interferences): The HES01 continuously validates magnetic data against GNSS-derived heading, detecting potential inconsistencies before they affect the navigation solution. This provides the autopilot with a reliable heading reference even in electromagnetically challenging environments.

articles.title: Klaipėda Port launches tender for Southern Port area
articles.summary: The Klaipėda State Seaport Authority has launched a tender to select future tenants for a new 100-hectare area in the southern part of the port, in a project worth more than EUR 1 billion. The aim is to attract strategic investors who will join the Authority from the outset to develop and deliver the project, […]
articles.body: The Klaipėda State Seaport Authority has launched a tender to select future tenants for a new 100-hectare area in the southern part of the port, in a project worth more than EUR 1 billion. The aim is to attract strategic investors who will join the Authority from the outset to develop and deliver the project, which is intended for cargo handling and maritime industry activities. Transport and Communications Minister Juras Taminskas called it the largest expansion of the Port of Klaipėda in the history of independent Lithuania, one that will strengthen competitiveness, generate billions of euros in value for the economy and improve regional security. The Authority will create 100 hectares of new land, build about 1.3 km of new quays, deepen part of the shipping channel in the southern port area, create a 600-metre-wide turning basin and provide road and rail connections. These works are estimated at around EUR 600 million, of which future tenants will contribute at least EUR 300 million if the whole territory is leased, with proportionate minimum contributions for bids covering only part of it. The indicative layout earmarks about 50 hectares for a container terminal with a full build-out capacity of about 1.5 million TEU, and the remaining 50 hectares for a wider range of port activities, with the final allocation depending on the tender outcome. Lease agreements will run for 50 years, and participants may bid for the whole area or a smaller part. Each bidder will offer an initial financial contribution based on the quay length and land area sought. At least half must be paid before the land is handed over, and the remainder within 15 years of possession. Tenants must also invest in their own buildings, cranes and equipment, and cargo-handling companies must commit to minimum annual cargo volumes that cannot decrease over the lease term. The tender will proceed in stages through the electronic platform Užsakovas. Applications and initial proposals will first be assessed against requirements covering technical capacity, professional experience and financial strength. Qualified participants will then enter a dialogue on technical, financial and legal terms before submitting final proposals. If any land remains after the first round, further rounds may be held. Each selected participant must pass a national security assessment before signing a lease. Director General Algis Latakas said a project of this scale calls for a different approach: the Authority is seeking partners who will invest in the new infrastructure from the start and later build facilities, docks and warehouses or install cranes, and it is working to attract major international cargo handling and maritime industry companies able to ensure stable cargo flows. The port currently has limited room to expand, which restricts its growth and its ability to remain a leading port. Construction preparation is already under way: Tilsta, contracted at EUR 24.5 million excluding VAT to build the southern port gates, has set up its site, and the new structures will also prevent saltwater from entering the Curonian Lagoon.

articles.title: US Ethanol Could Fuel Methanol-Ready Ships, Study Finds
articles.summary: Ethanol could be used to fuel a growing fleet of methanol-capable ships with limited modifications to existing dual-fuel engines and bunkering infrastructure, offering an alternative as supplies of low-emission methanol remain constrained, according to a new industry study.The study…
articles.body: US Ethanol Could Fuel Methanol-Ready Ships, Study Finds Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 12, 2026 Clarence Woo, Managing Director of the Global Centre for Green Fuels (Credit: GCGF) Ethanol could be used to fuel a growing fleet of methanol-capable ships with limited modifications to existing dual-fuel engines and bunkering infrastructure, offering an alternative as supplies of low-emission methanol remain constrained, according to a new industry study. The study, published by the Maritime Ethanol & Methanol Alliance (MEMA), a platform of the Global Centre for Green Fuels (GCGF), found that ethanol could support more than 300 methanol-capable vessels currently in service or on order, either independently or blended with methanol. The United States has approximately 2 billion gallons of spare annual ethanol production capacity, with plants capable of producing 18.5 billion gallons compared with output of 16.4 billion gallons in 2025, the report said. The country produces just over half of the world's fuel ethanol and exports to around 80 countries, largely through Gulf Coast terminals that also serve as major bunkering hubs. According to the study's illustrative scenarios, supplying ethanol equivalent to 1% of international shipping's annual fuel consumption by mass would require approximately 1 billion gallons, while a 5% share by the mid-2030s would need around 5 billion gallons. “Ethanol is moving beyond pilots, and this study shows the United States has the production base and export infrastructure to supply shipping at scale. The next challenge is consistency. As international bunkering grows, shipping needs standardised and fungible marine fuel specifications, together with traceable feedstocks and a robust chain of custody, so that ethanol from different producers and regions can be used with confidence," said Clarence Woo, Managing Director of GCGF. The report comes as ethanol bunkering begins moving beyond trials. On September 28, Tangier Maersk completed a commercial ship-to-ship bunkering of US corn ethanol in Houston, described as the first publicly announced US ethanol bunkering operation involving a deep-sea container vessel. The study assessed ethanol at technology readiness level 8–9, indicating technical maturity with commercial deployment emerging. Compared with heavy fuel oil, ethanol virtually eliminates sulphur oxide emissions and could reduce nitrogen oxide emissions by 40–94% and particulate matter by 90–99%, depending on engine technology, according to the report. It also estimated ethanol's net production cost, after co-product revenue, at below $1 per gallon, while identifying the need for standardised marine fuel specifications and traceable supply chains to support wider international adoption. ABS provided the technical analysis as knowledge partner, while US ethanol producer Marquis Energy contributed industry input. The study's views and recommendations are those of MEMA.

articles.title: Singapore Seeks LNG Floating Storage Operators to Expand Bunkering Ops
articles.summary: The Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) has opened applications for licenses to operate up to two liquefied natural gas (LNG) floating storage units (FSUs) in Singapore anchorages, aiming to expand LNG bunkering capacity and strengthen…
articles.body: Singapore Seeks LNG Floating Storage Operators to Expand Bunkering Ops Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 12, 2026 © Jelena / Adobe Stock The Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) has opened applications for licenses to operate up to two liquefied natural gas (LNG) floating storage units (FSUs) in Singapore anchorages, aiming to expand LNG bunkering capacity and strengthen supply resilience. The initiative follows the award of eight new LNG bunker supplier licences in July 2026 and is intended to diversify LNG storage and reloading options. Applications are open to existing LNG bunker licensees, which may partner with third-party terminal operators to provide storage and operational expertise. Applicants must own or charter at least one FSU with a minimum storage capacity of 130,000 cubic metres, registered with the Singapore Registry of Ships. Most of each unit's storage capacity must be allocated to LNG bunkering, with a minimum portion made available to other LNG bunker suppliers on open-access terms. The vessels must comply with MPA's safety and operational requirements, while operators will be required to disclose their intended maximum fees for LNG reloading services. Each licence will be valid for five years. The FSUs must also hold International Sustainability and Carbon Certification European Union (ISCC-EU) certification to handle bio-LNG and e-LNG, supporting the future supply of these lower-emission alternatives. MPA will hold an applicant briefing on December 4, 2026, with applications due by 5 p.m. on February 4, 2027.

articles.body: Ports & Infrastructure November 12, 2026 · 10 minutes ago Port of Gothenburg eyes large-scale biogas bunkering in 2027 Sweden’s Port of Gothenburg is gearing up to launch a new LBG liquefaction plant next year to enable large-scale liquefied biogas bunkering. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Artist’s impression of Nordion Energi’s biogas liquefaction plant at the Port of Gothenburg Source: Port of Gothenburg The Port of Gothenburg, which is perceived as the largest port in the Nordic countries, has tucked a new green transition milestone under its belt with the installation of a 500-cubic-meter storage tank for liquefied biogas (LBG). Built and owned by Nordion Energi and scheduled to open in the second quarter of 2027, Sweden's first grid-connected biogas liquefaction plant is set to unlock large-scale renewable bunkering for the shipping industry and supercharge the local green fuel value chain. The construction milestone for the biogas liquefaction plant at the Port of Gothenburg comes as the facility’s storage tank for LBG got installed. This renewable fuel with low climate impact is said to have the ability to replace fossil alternatives in several sectors. As a result, the interest in the fuel is growing rapidly, particularly in shipping. " Shipping’s transition requires a collaborative value chain. This facility strengthens the port’s position in renewable bunker fuels and makes it possible to offer LBG to the shipping sector on a larger scale. As we see more and more vessels on order for LBG operation, we also see strong potential for increased bunkering at the Port of Gothenburg. " — Therese Jällbrink Head of Renewable Energy at the Port of Gothenburg According to the Port of Gothenburg, groundworks, including foundations and base slabs, have been completed, and the LBG tank is the first of the plant’s key components to be installed. The tank, which arrived at the European port by vessel, has a volume of 500 cubic meters and weighs close to 140 tonnes. It will be able to store up to 200 tonnes of LBG once the facility is operational. Related Articles Alternative Fuels Port of Gothenburg hosts Swedish-produced biomethane bunkering pilot 2 min read " This is an important milestone. The facility is now really starting to take shape, and we are moving closer to our goal of being able to deliver LBG from the gas grid to shipping, heavy transport and industry. " — Carolina Wistén Head of Customer and Market, Gas Grid, at Nordion Energi The liquefaction plant, which will be the first in Sweden to be directly connected to the west Swedish gas grid, will create a new market for Swedish biogas producers that are, or want to become, connected to the gas grid. This facility, which is expected to be completed in the second quarter of 2027, will be capable of delivering 250 gigawatt-hours of LBG annually, equivalent to the consumption of 500 trucks or the bunkering of 50 vessels. articles.body: Wallem Group has appointed Apostolos Poulovassilis as General Manager, Ship Management, Greece, as the company moves to expand its ship management business in the Greek market. The appointment takes effect in November 2026 and forms part of Wallem’s strategy to strengthen its relationships with Greek shipowners and develop its regional operations. In the newly established role, Poulovassilis will oversee the development of Wallem’s Greece office, focusing on business growth, client relationships and the expansion of the group’s ship management services. He will report directly to Ioannis Stefanou, Managing Director, Ship Management, at Wallem Group. Extensive experience in ship management Poulovassilis brings more than 35 years of international maritime experience, covering ship management, classification and maritime technology. He began his career as a marine engineer before joining Lloyd’s Register, where he spent 25 years in technical and management positions. His responsibilities included senior leadership roles covering Greece and Europe. He subsequently served as Chief Operating Officer at Eletson Corporation and Chief Executive Officer at Aegean Shipping Management. More recently, he held a senior leadership position at Ocean Technologies Group/OneOcean, focusing on maritime digital solutions, commercial development and strategic client relationships. John Rowley, CEO of Wallem Group, said the appointment supports the company’s plans to strengthen its presence in Greece. He highlighted Poulovassilis’ experience across ship classification, fleet management and maritime technology, alongside his established relationships within the Greek shipping industry. The new general manager will be responsible for developing business opportunities and expanding Wallem’s relationships with shipowners and other maritime stakeholders. The appointment reflects Wallem’s plans to develop its ship management activities in Greece, although the company has not announced specific fleet management contracts or operational targets for the new office.Wallem

articles.body: Americas Environment Operations Tech US ethanol industry eyes growing marine fuel market Bojan Lepic November 12, 2026 0 123 1 minute read WinGD WinGD Ethanol could emerge as an alternative marine fuel for the growing fleet of methanol-capable ships, with existing engines and bunkering infrastructure requiring only limited modifications, according to a new industry study. The report, Marine Ethanol: Unlocking the US Opportunity , published by the Maritime Ethanol & Methanol Alliance (MEMA), says the fuel could support more than 300 methanol-capable vessels currently operating or on order, either independently or blended with methanol. The study identifies the US as a potential major supplier, with annual ethanol production capacity of 18.5bn gallons compared with 16.4bn gallons in 2025, leaving about 2bn gallons of spare capacity. According to the report, supplying just 1% of shipping’s annual fuel consumption would require around 1bn gallons of ethanol. Increasing that share to 5% by the mid-2030s would require approximately 5bn gallons. The findings follow Maersk’s first commercial ship-to-ship bunkering of US-produced corn ethanol aboard its dual-fuel containership Tangier Maersk in Houston in September. The study also highlights potential environmental benefits, estimating reductions of 40% to 94% in nitrogen oxide emissions and 90% to 99% in particulate matter compared with heavy fuel oil, depending on engine technology. Clarence Woo, managing director of the Global Centre for Green Fuels, said the US already had the production capacity and export infrastructure to supply ethanol to shipping at scale. However, he stressed the need for standardised marine fuel specifications, traceable feedstocks and reliable certification systems. The study, developed with technical input from ABS, comes ahead of renewed International Maritime Organization discussions on its proposed Net-Zero Framework in December. articles.title: Ship Breaking: Dry Bulk Scrapping Falls 18-year Low
articles.summary: "Between January and October 2026, dry bulk ship recycling fell 36% y/y to 3m DWT, its lowest level in 18 years. Only 70 ships were recycled, primarily smaller ships in the handysize and supramax segments, as strong freight rates have extended the operational lives of older ships…
articles.body: Ship Breaking: Dry Bulk Scrapping Falls 18-year Low Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 12, 2026 Chart courtesy BIMCO "Between January and October 2026, dry bulk ship recycling fell 36% y/y to 3m DWT, its lowest level in 18 years. Only 70 ships were recycled, primarily smaller ships in the handysize and supramax segments, as strong freight rates have extended the operational lives of older ships,” says Filipe Gouveia, Shipping Analysis Manager at BIMCO. Dry bulk ship recycling has been at a low level since 2021 due to strong freight rates. Several disruptions have tightened the supply/demand balance. These include high congestion in 2021, longer sailing distances due to sanctions on Russian coal, which caused ships to be rerouted away from the Red Sea, and growing shipments from the Atlantic to Asia. More recently, strong investment in AI has supported electricity demand, coal consumption and global economic growth, helping the market withstand headwinds from changes in US trade policy and disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. “Following several years of low ship recycling levels, a significant overhang has built up. We estimate that if ship lifecycles had remained in line with those observed between 2000 and 2019, an additional 856 ships, totalling 61m DWT, would have been recycled by now. That is equivalent to 6% of the current fleet capacity. As ships remain in service for longer, the dry bulk fleet has gradually aged, with the average bulk carrier now over 13 years old, compared with an average of 10 years at the start of the decade,” says Gouveia. The recycling overhang is increasingly visible in the age profile of the fleet. There are now 1,035 dry bulk ships, totalling 46.7m DWT, which are more than 25 years old. These are equivalent to 7% of ships and 4% of fleet capacity. The share of older capacity is highest in the handysize and panamax segments, at 8% each, compared with 5% for supramax. By contrast, only 11 capesize ships are more than 25 years old, since capesizes typically have shorter lifecycles. In our latest Dry Bulk Shipping Market Overview & Outlook, we forecast the supply/demand balance to gradually weaken in 2027 and 2028, albeit from a high baseline. Ship deliveries are expected to accelerate, growing 19% in 2027 and a further 4% in 2028. The increase will be driven by the capesize segment, following higher contracting in recent years. “As market conditions gradually weaken, freight rates could soften, making it less attractive to keep older ships operating. Consequently, we estimate ship recycling could increase to 5.5m DWT in 2027 and 9.2m DWT in 2028, which would be the highest since 2020. Nevertheless, even with this increase, recycling levels would be low compared with the highs seen during the 2010s and an overhang of older ships would remain,” says Gouveia.

articles.title: Xiamen Port launches green methanol bunkering with OOCL WISDOM
articles.summary: Xiamen Port in China has completed its first ship-to-ship green methanol bunkering operation, supplying 1,005 tonnes of the alternative marine fuel to OOCL WISDOM, one of the world’s largest methanol dual-fuel container vessels. The operation took place on 4 November at Xiamen Yuanhai Container Terminal, marking the...
articles.body: Xiamen Port in China has completed its first ship-to-ship green methanol bunkering operation, supplying 1,005 tonnes of the alternative marine fuel to OOCL WISDOM, one of the world’s largest methanol dual-fuel container vessels. The operation took place on 4 November at Xiamen Yuanhai Container Terminal, marking the first green methanol ship-to-ship bunkering operation in China’s Fujian province and expanding the port’s capabilities in alternative marine fuel supply. According to COSCO SHIPPING, the bunkering operation is estimated to deliver a reduction of more than 1,600 tonnes of carbon emissions compared with the use of conventional marine fuels. OOCL WISDOM receives 1,005 tonnes of green methanol The 24,168-TEU OOCL WISDOM is the first of seven methanol dual-fuel container vessels being introduced into OOCL’s fleet and operates on the carrier’s Asia–North Europe Loop 1 (LL1) service. The vessel previously completed its first green methanol bunkering operation at Qingdao Port in July 2026, before commencing its maiden commercial voyage to Europe. The latest operation at Xiamen represents a milestone for the port rather than the vessel, establishing the facility’s ability to provide green methanol through ship-to-ship fuel transfers. According to information released by local port authorities, green methanol can reduce lifecycle carbon emissions by more than 85% compared with conventional marine fuels, depending on its production pathway and associated emissions. Xiamen expands alternative fuel bunkering capabilities The successful operation adds green methanol to Xiamen Port’s existing alternative fuel bunkering capabilities, which also include liquefied natural gas (LNG) and biofuels. The development is intended to strengthen the port’s ability to serve container vessels equipped with alternative fuel propulsion systems as shipping companies expand their dual-fuel fleets. COSCO SHIPPING said it would continue developing green marine fuel bunkering services through its activities in port operations, shipping and fuel supply. Local port authorities are also working to improve operational standards and safety procedures to support the transition from initial green methanol bunkering operations to regular commercial services.

articles.title: Sealartec Wins USCG Contract to Test Autonomous LARS
articles.summary: Technology previously demonstrated aboard the U.S. Navy's Stiletto test platform will advance to operational evaluation aboard a Legend-class National Security Cutter.Israel-based maritime technology company Sealartec has secured a U.S. Coast…
articles.body: Sealartec Wins USCG Contract to Test Autonomous LARS Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 12, 2026 USCGC Midgett, a Legend-class National Security Cutter. U.S. Coast Guard photo; source file supplied by Sealartec. Technology previously demonstrated aboard the U.S. Navy's Stiletto test platform will advance to operational evaluation aboard a Legend-class National Security Cutter. Israel-based maritime technology company Sealartec has secured a U.S. Coast Guard contract under the Foreign Comparative Testing (FCT) Program to supply its ALR-S autonomous launch and recovery system for installation, testing and operational assessment aboard a Legend-class National Security Cutter (NSC). The award advances the technology from an experimental U.S. Navy platform to a structured evaluation aboard one of the Coast Guard's largest and most capable cutters, targeting one of the more challenging aspects of maritime operations: safely recovering small boats onto moving vessels in increasingly difficult sea conditions. Sealartec's ALR-S technology is designed to automate the stern-ramp recovery process, reducing the need for manual intervention while minimizing the risks associated with relative motion between a small boat and its host vessel. During conventional stern-ramp recovery operations, wave action and differences in vessel movement can generate significant impact loads, potentially damaging equipment, injuring personnel and limiting the conditions under which recovery can be safely performed. ALR-S addresses these challenges by autonomously controlling the interaction between the recovering boat and the ship's stern ramp, with the objective of improving recovery consistency, reducing impact forces and expanding the operational envelope. The Coast Guard evaluation builds on a June 2025 demonstration aboard Stiletto, the U.S. Navy's Joint Prototyping and Experimentation Maritime test platform, in Norfolk, Virginia. Stiletto, the U.S. Navy JPEM test platform. U.S. Navy photo by Travis Troller / NSWC Carderock Division. During that demonstration, Sealartec's technology autonomously managed the capture and recovery sequence after a small boat approached the vessel's stern and matched its speed. U.S. Coast Guard personnel also participated in the demonstration. The new contract will see a complete ALR-S system provided for installation and assessment aboard a Legend-class cutter. While autonomous launch and recovery is particularly relevant to the expanding use of uncrewed surface vessels, Sealartec maintains that the technology offers significant benefits for conventional crewed boats as well. Automating launch and recovery is increasingly viewed as a necessary component of autonomous maritime operations. Even vessels capable of independently navigating and executing missions remain dependent on personnel if their deployment and retrieval require manual intervention. "We are honored to partner with the U.S. Coast Guard under the FCT framework," said Amitai Peleg, Co-Founder and CEO of Sealartec. "Stern-ramp recovery systems are widely used, yet all face the same challenge: safe recovery as sea states rise. While autonomous launch and recovery is essential for uncrewed systems, it can significantly improve manned recovery operations as well." The Foreign Comparative Testing Program evaluates mature technologies developed by allied nations against U.S. military requirements, providing a pathway to assess commercially developed systems without beginning a new development program. For Sealartec, the contract represents an opportunity to demonstrate ALR-S in an operational Coast Guard environment and gather performance data that could inform future procurement decisions. The company also develops autonomous connection technologies for refueling and replenishment, addressing other shipboard operations that remain dependent on human intervention. The Coast Guard contract does not constitute a fleet-wide procurement commitment, but establishes a formal evaluation process for determining the technology's suitability for future operations.

articles.summary: A new liquefied biogas (LBG) facility under construction at the Port of Gothenburg is scheduled to begin operations in the second quarter of 2027, providing a new source of renewable marine fuel for vessels calling at Scandinavia's largest port.The project…
articles.body: Future Fuel: Port LBG Bunkering Facility on Track for 2027 Open Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 12, 2026 Artist’s impression of Nordion Energi’s biogas liquefaction plant at the Port of Gothenburg. The storage tank is now in place, bringing the facility one step closer to completion. Image: Port of Gothenburg. A new liquefied biogas (LBG) facility under construction at the Port of Gothenburg is scheduled to begin operations in the second quarter of 2027, providing a new source of renewable marine fuel for vessels calling at Scandinavia's largest port. The project, developed and owned by Swedish energy infrastructure company Nordion Energi, recently reached a construction milestone with the installation of its 500-cubic-meter LBG storage tank. The tank, which arrived at the port by ship, weighs approximately 140 tonnes and will have the capacity to store up to 200 tonnes of liquefied biogas. Once operational, the facility will be capable of producing 250 gigawatt-hours of LBG annually, equivalent to the fuel requirements of approximately 500 heavy-duty trucks or the bunkering needs of 50 vessels. The plant will be the first biogas liquefaction facility in Sweden directly connected to the western Swedish gas grid, creating a new route for domestically produced biogas to reach maritime, transportation and industrial customers. For the Port of Gothenburg, the investment represents another step toward establishing the port as a regional hub for alternative marine fuels. "Shipping's transition requires a collaborative value chain. This facility strengthens the port's position in renewable bunker fuels and makes it possible to offer LBG to the shipping sector on a larger scale," said Therese Jällbrink, Head of Renewable Energy at the Port of Gothenburg. "As we see more and more vessels on order for LBG operation, we also see strong potential for increased bunkering at the Port of Gothenburg." LBG offers a renewable alternative to conventional fossil fuels and can be used by vessels equipped with compatible gas-fueled propulsion systems. Its availability is becoming increasingly relevant as shipowners invest in alternative-fuel tonnage to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. The project also provides opportunities for Swedish biogas producers connected to the national gas infrastructure. ST1 Biokraft has already secured a portion of the facility's future liquefaction capacity, while several shipping companies regularly calling at Gothenburg currently operate LBG-fueled vessels. Groundworks, foundations and base slabs have been completed, with installation of the storage tank marking the first major equipment milestone. "The facility is now really starting to take shape, and we are moving closer to our goal of being able to deliver LBG from the gas grid to shipping, heavy transport and industry," said Carolina Wistén, Head of Customer and Market, Gas Grid, at Nordion Energi. The Port of Gothenburg handles approximately 20% of Sweden's foreign trade and more than half of its container traffic, making it a significant location for expanding renewable marine fuel infrastructure.

articles.body: MSC Mediterranean Shipping Company has recorded stronger growth since the spring of 2026, particularly on trades originating in Asia, according to CEO Søren Toft, who outlined the carrier’s performance, ongoing investments and operational challenges as the year approaches its end. In a business update shared on LinkedIn following the third quarter, Toft described 2026 as a year marked by contrasting market conditions, with a more moderate start followed by stronger activity. “It’s been a year of two halves. After a more moderate start to the year, we have seen strong growth since the spring, particularly out of Asia,” said Søren Toft, CEO of MSC Mediterranean Shipping Company. The update comes as MSC continues expanding its global shipping network, vessel capacity and logistics operations, while navigating geopolitical uncertainty and persistent congestion at major ports. MSC continues fleet and network expansion Toft confirmed that MSC’s fleet now comprises more than 1,000 container vessels, reflecting the company’s continued investment in shipping capacity and network development. The carrier is also expanding its LNG dual-fuel fleet, with its combined capacity expected to exceed 4 million TEU in the coming years. The projection represents a significant part of MSC’s ongoing investment in alternative-fuel vessel technology. Beyond its container fleet, MSC continues strengthening its global service network through additional capacity and new services. The company’s investment activities also extend to port terminals and inland logistics. Toft highlighted a new terminal in Morocco as part of MSC’s expansion of its terminal operations, alongside continued development of its inland logistics activities. MSC has also placed new vessel orders to expand its car carrier fleet, further broadening the group’s activities beyond container shipping. Port congestion and geopolitical uncertainty remain key challenges Despite the stronger growth recorded since the spring, Toft acknowledged that the shipping industry continues to face significant operational challenges. “Port congestion has become a new normal in our industry, and geopolitical uncertainty remains,” he said. The MSC chief executive emphasised the importance of maintaining flexibility and operational focus to ensure reliable services for customers amid changing market conditions. Port congestion and geopolitical developments continue to complicate shipping network planning, requiring carriers to adapt their operations as conditions evolve across international trade routes. Nevertheless, Toft expressed confidence in MSC’s position heading into the final weeks of 2026. “Overall, we navigate a volatile world with good momentum,” he said.

Europe accounted for 81% of Yamal’s recorded deliveries, underscoring the project’s continued dependence on the market it is about to lose. The estimated bill is around 21% higher than the €7.2 billion calculated for all of 2025 . The figures are indicative estimates based on monthly benchmark gas prices and delivered volumes, rather than verified contract payments. But the more immediate challenge for Yamal LNG, operated by Russian producer Novatek, is logistical. The EU ban on Russian LNG imports under eligible existing long-term contracts takes effect on January 1, forcing the project to redirect cargoes toward Asia just as winter ice makes eastbound navigation along the Northern Sea Route increasingly difficult. A Kpler analysis by principal commodity shipping analyst Igor Gavri? suggests there is still room for several additional European deliveries before the deadline. Based on vessel positions, historical movements, port restrictions and assumed sailing speeds, a tanker loading at Sabetta could theoretically complete around three additional deliveries to Zeebrugge before January 1. With transshipment to a conventional LNG carrier near Murmansk an Arc7 vessel could complete 4-5 additional deliveries. Russia has assembled a growing fleet of aging LNG vessels ahead of the ban. Kpler’s accompanying rotation model assumes 17 knots and four days in port per cycle. The analysis identifies plant output, rather than tanker availability, as the principal constraint on additional shipments. The deadline will produce a sharp change in a shipping system built around relatively short European voyages. Yamal depends on 14 specialized Arc7 ice-class LNG carriers, which can operate in Arctic waters and return quickly from nearby European terminals. During winter, conventional LNG carriers cannot reach Sabetta, while direct eastbound voyages to Asia become considerably more demanding. Since 2018, only 11 Arc7 cargoes have traveled east through the Northern Sea Route between November and May, Urgewald said. Russia is preparing to change that pattern. Rosatom expects regular year-round eastbound shipping along the Northern Sea Route to begin in early 2027 , coinciding with the arrival of an additional nuclear icebreaker and efforts by major exporters to establish regular deliveries to Asian markets. The nuclear-powered icebreaker Chukotka , the fourth serial Project 22220 vessel, is scheduled to enter service early next year, bringing Russia’s operational nuclear icebreaker fleet to nine. One likely operating model for Novatek and state-owned Atomflot is to use nuclear icebreakers to escort convoys of multiple Arc7 LNG carriers, improving the efficiency of scarce icebreaking capacity. After the European ban, Murmansk ship-to-ship transshipment and conventional LNG carriers are also expected to play a larger role , allowing Arc7 vessels to return to Sabetta rather than undertaking longer voyages to Asian customers. The transition to year-round eastbound NSR deliveries is far from guaranteed. Russia previously targeted year-round eastbound navigation for 2024 but failed to establish regular service. March and April remain particularly difficult, and a single additional icebreaker alone will not resolve constraints involving convoy speeds and icebreaker redundancy. October deliveries to Europe totaled 705,591 tonnes across 10 cargoes, worth an estimated €839 million. France received seven shipments, while Spain and the Netherlands received two and one, respectively. The January ban will not necessarily stop Yamal LNG exports, but it will remove the project’s most convenient winter market. European firms will be permitted to continue transporting and selling Yamal products outside of the EU. An earlier proposed complete ban on providing services to the Russian LNG sector was subsequently weakened by the EU. articles.summary: The maritime energy transition will require support for human capacity development across developing States, including SIDS and LDCS, as well as investment in scalable and bankable projects that will support the move to zero emission shipping by or around 20250, in line with IMO’s GHG Strategy.
