articles.body: Financing the maritime energy transition in International Shipping News 12/11/2026 The maritime energy transition will require support for human capacity development across developing States, including SIDS and LDCS, as well as investment in scalable and bankable projects that will support the move to zero emission shipping by or around 20250, in line with IMO’s GHG Strategy. During an IMO Future Fuels and Technology Project session on “Maritime Infrastructure and the Global Energy Transition: From Supply to Deployment” in Busan, Republic of Korea (29 October), IMO’s Sonakshi Mishra highlighted IMO’s holistic approach to technical cooperation to help bridge financing gaps and achieve sustainable, long-term impacts, through the FINSMART+ and GHG-SMART projects. FINSMART+ is a recently launched GEF project which IMO is executing in collaboration with EBRD and The World Bank Group. It aims to advance maritime decarbonization projects, including existing IMO technical cooperation projects related to national action plans, pilots and feasibility studies – supporting them towards investment readiness by facilitating partnerships and matchmaking with potential financiers. GHG-SMART is supporting capacity development in climate finance and project development, while generating knowledge base on climate finance in the maritime sector. A new study, currently being finalized under the GHG-SMART programme, will assess for the first time, climate finance flows across the maritime sector and identify financing gaps and opportunities. The findings aim to inform efforts to improve access to finance for the maritime energy transition, particularly in developing countries, including small island developing States (SIDS) and least developed countries (LDCs). Closing the financing gap requires strengthening maritime administrations’ capacity to prepare bankable proposals, integrating maritime priorities into national climate, energy and investment plans, and aggregating demand across sectors and, particularly for SIDS, regionally to achieve economies of scale. The IMO Future Fuels and Technology Project session was delivered in collaboration with Ministry of Ocean and Fisheries (MOF) of the Republic of Korea as part of the Decarbonization Forum, in Busan (29 October) during Korean Maritime Week. IMO’s Seungjun Seo presented the expansive data available on the IMO Future Fuels and Technology website. The event was attended by more than 400 people, including representatives from governments, international organisations, financial institutions, industry, academia, research institutions and port authorities. articles.title: CII forecast showing a D? How to improve your rating before year-end
articles.summary: The CII grade for a year is calculated from that year’s verified data. That is why the grade cannot be managed after the year ends, and also why a D forecast in the middle of the year is a decision point and not a verdict. Every voyage still to be sailed adds to the result. ...
articles.body: CII forecast showing a D? How to improve your rating before year-end in International Shipping News 12/11/2026 The CII grade for a year is calculated from that year’s verified data. That is why the grade cannot be managed after the year ends, and also why a D forecast in the middle of the year is a decision point and not a verdict. Every voyage still to be sailed adds to the result. This post is a playbook for that moment. It assumes you already know what CII is and how the A to E scale works. If not, start with What is CII in shipping? and CII compliance in shipping. Confirm the forecast is built on clean data A forecast is only as good as the fuel and distance figures behind it. Before changing how a ship is run, check that consumption has been reported correctly and that fuel used for purposes other than propulsion is allocated properly. On tankers, sub-consumers such as cargo heating, cargo transfer pumps, inert gas systems, auxiliary boilers, generators and ballast water treatment can account for a substantial share of fuel use, and accurate allocation can lead to a fairer CII assessment. The full picture is in How to improve tanker CII scores with verified fuel reporting. Find out whether the ship or the bar moved The required CII tightens every year. It started at 5% below the 2019 baseline in 2023, reaches 11% below by 2026, and from 2027 tightens by 2.625% a year, reaching 21.5% below baseline by 2030. A ship that earned a C last year and changes nothing can drop to a D because the requirement moved while the ship stood still. This matters because the fix is different. If the ship has genuinely become less efficient, look at hull condition, speed and routing. If only the bar has moved, the ship needs to improve just to hold its grade, and the plan has to include permanent changes, not one-off savings. The calculation behind both sides of the comparison is in How is CII calculated? Choose levers by how fast they act Every lever works the same way: emit less CO₂ for the same transport work. They differ in how quickly they can be used. Speed is the fastest. Modest reductions cut fuel consumption disproportionately, and speed can be changed on the next voyage, subject to the commercial deadline. Routing and weather choices also act voyage by voyage, avoiding fuel burned fighting conditions. Hull and propeller condition act more slowly, because cleaning has to be scheduled. A fouled or degraded hull increases resistance and raises fuel consumption, and it drifts gradually between dry-docking cycles, so periodic assessments often catch it late. Scheduling hull cleaning and propeller polishing around trade patterns and port availability, using continuous monitoring, is what lets the work happen before the rating suffers. See The compliance advantage: AI agents, hull performance and the CII stakes. Cargo and ballast planning improves the ratio directly, through fewer empty legs and better utilisation, but it depends on the trade the ship is in. Protect the commercial side A rating that slips can have commercial consequences well before any regulatory one. Charterers screen on ratings, some charter parties carry CII clauses, and a vessel that drops a letter rating during a charter can trigger contractual penalties. That makes the decision about how to recover the grade a shared one between owner and charterer. Slowing down is not always free. In a high market, the time lost can cost more than the fuel saved, so the choice has to balance bunker costs, market rates and the rating together. Simulating the CII impact of a voyage before it begins, and choosing routes and speeds that meet the commercial deadline while protecting the rating, is the practical way to do that. For the charterer’s view, see How voyage optimisation protects margins in a CII-driven market. If the ship is still heading for an E or a third D A single E rating, or a D three years in a row, requires a corrective action plan showing how the ship will return to C or better, approved as part of its energy-efficiency management plan. There is no direct IMO fine, but the commercial costs arrive sooner. If the forecast says a ship will land in that group, start drafting the plan while there is still time to act on it, and use the same data and simulations to show what each measure is expected to change. Where ZeroNorth fits ZeroNorth’s Emission Analytics gives operators real-time insight into CII performance, including the year-to-date rating, and simulates future ratings. It alerts an operator or manager when a vessel is at risk of becoming non-compliant, and suggests alternative voyage routes that balance commercial objectives with carbon emissions. The bottom line The grade is set by the whole year, so a D forecast during the year is the best time to act on it. Check the data, work out whether the ship or the requirement moved, use the fastest levers first, protect the charter terms, and prepare the corrective action plan early if the ship is heading for one. articles.body: Pacific Environment Welcomes Ulsan Port’s Commercial e-Ammonia Bunkering Milestone in International Shipping News 12/11/2026 On October 25–26, Ulsan Port Authority (UPA), together with Lotte Fine Chemical, HD Hyundai Heavy Industries, Shinheungsa, and Eastern Pacific Shipping (EPS), supplied 800 tonnes of renewable energy-based e-ammonia to Terra Clove, a newly launched 93,000 m3 Very Large Ammonia Carrier (VLAC) at Ulsan Port. The fuel was supplied through a Port-to-Ship (PTS) bunkering system connecting the port’s onshore infrastructure directly to the vessel. The operation represents Korea’s first demonstration of commercial-scale ammonia bunkering at a domestic port. It follows three earlier ammonia fueling demonstrations conducted at Ulsan Port this year and further strengthens the port’s experience in safely handling next-generation marine fuels. The milestone comes as Ulsan Port advances an ambitious strategy to become a leading clean energy and marine fuel hub in Northeast Asia. Under UPA’s long-term vision, the port plans to expand infrastructure for hydrogen and ammonia, strengthen methanol terminal capacity, and develop markets for next-generation marine fuels. Reactions from Ulsan Port Authority BYEON Jaeyoung, President of Ulsan Port Authority, said, “This project was a clear demonstration of the importance of strong collaboration and coordination with relevant authorities and industry partners to advance ammonia bunkering operations at Ulsan Port and in South Korea,” And he added, We will continue to promote ammonia ship fuel supply in cooperation with related institutions and companies to ensure Ulsan Port establishes itself as a hub for supplying eco-friendly ship fuel.” KIM Byunggu, Director of the Sustainable Energy & Environment Department at Ulsan Port Authority, added, “We will strengthen cooperation with industry partners and related organizations to expand ammonia bunkering infrastructure and support the transition to cleaner shipping fuels.” Ulsan Port Authority is also taking concrete steps to accelerate the adoption of alternative marine fuels through financial incentives and port infrastructure support. In 2026, UPA introduced a new incentive program offering shipping companies up to KRW 10 million per vessel for bunkering eligible fuels, including methanol, ammonia, hydrogen, and LNG. While it is disappointing that LNG remains eligible for these incentives, the program represents an opportunity to encourage the uptake of cleaner marine fuels. Looking ahead, prioritizing zero- and near-zero-emission (ZNZ) fuels will be essential to ensuring that public incentives support the long-term decarbonization of shipping and strengthen Ulsan Port’s leadership in the clean energy transition. Reactions from Pacific Environment Pacific Environment, which joined the memorandum of understanding with UPA on accelerating Green Shipping Corridors and maritime fuel transition in 2024, sees successful commercial e-ammonia bunkering as an opportunity to connect these efforts with accelerating Green Shipping Corridors and the energy transition in and around the port area. Kim Mikyoung, Country Director for the Republic of Korea at Pacific Environment, said, “We congratulate Ulsan Port Authority and its partners on this important milestone. Supplying e-ammonia to an oceangoing vessel at a commercial scale makes it clear that the shift to clean marine fuels is no longer a question of technology, but a question of time. It also sends a strong signal to Korea’s ports and shipping industry that ports are evolving from logistics gateways into energy hubs, and that the infrastructure needed for ZNZ fuel transition has begun to take shape. Other Korean ports must now move quickly to prepare for ZNZ fuels.” Kang Hyunju, Climate Campaign Director, Asia, at Pacific Environment, said, “Building on its progress in methanol and now ammonia bunkering, Ulsan Port has a great opportunity to position itself as a leading clean marine fuel hub in Asia. We hope to see Ulsan go even further, evolving into an integrated energy hub powered by renewable energy and playing a leading role in both shipping decarbonization and the broader clean energy transition.” The future of Korea’s maritime transition Pacific Environment believes the next phase of Korea’s maritime transition should focus on creating stronger synergies between shipping demand and clean energy investment. Growing demand for ZNZ marine fuels can stimulate investment in renewable electricity, green hydrogen, and hydrogen derivatives, while diversifying Korea’s future energy supply and strengthening energy security. Policies such as differentiated port incentives based on lifecycle greenhouse gas performance, long-term fuel offtake agreements, sustainability certification, and targeted support for early green shipping corridors can help bridge the cost gap between conventional and zero-emission fuels. Ulsan’s latest achievement provides an important foundation for this transition. Pacific Environment looks forward to working with Ulsan Port Authority, government agencies, shipping companies, fuel producers, and other partners to connect Ulsan and other Korean ports with international green shipping corridors, while ensuring that maritime decarbonization becomes a driver of renewable energy growth, local economic opportunity, greater energy security, and cleaner air for port communities. Source: Pacific Environment 2026-11-12 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Monjasa adds five sister tankers in major fleet renewal deal in International Shipping News 12/11/2026 Global oil and shipping group, Monjasa is adding five sister tankers to its fleet in the company’s largestever tonnage acquisition, strengthening its activities in West Africa and providing greater flexibility across its global marine fuels supply operations. The deal comprises five 16,621-dwt product tankers from German shipowner Bernhard Schulte, as part of the ongoing fleet renewal strategy and continued investments in reliable supply infrastructure. The first four tankers, Monjasa Tracer, Monjasa Tuner, Monjasa Twister and Monjasa Tracker have already been delivered and deployed in West Africa and Northwest Europe. The remaining vessel, Monjasa Trigger, is scheduled for delivery by end of November 2026. Largest-ever tonnage acquisition in Monjasa “We are always looking at fleet renewal opportunities, but we are also very selective about where we invest. Finding five sister vessels of this quality, at competitive market terms and with an operating profile that fits our existing fleet, is not something you come across every day. This is the largest single tonnage acquisition in our history and it provides us more flexibility, strengthens our supply capabilities and keeps ensuring a solid platform for serving our customers in the years ahead,” says Group CEO, Anders Østergaard. Five sister vessels bring operational benefits The acquisitions follow another active year in which Monjasa completed a total of 16,741 marine fuels operations in 2025. With a deadweight capacity of 16,621 tonnes each, the newly acquired vessels will strengthen the company’s ability to serve different markets and adapt its fleet deployment to changing patterns in global demand. “Owning vessels is not just about adding more tonnage. It’s about having the right vessels available in the right markets and being able to operate them efficiently over time. The fact that these are five sister vessels is particularly attractive to us. We know the operating cost structure, we understand the technical requirements and we can build on the experience and capabilities already established within our ship management organisation,” Anders Østergaard concludes. Initially, the new tankers will strengthen Monjasa’s West African operations, while also providing opportunities for commercial freight trading and future deployment elsewhere in the group’s global supply network. All five tankers delivered before year-end The involved vessels are delivered in Rotterdam and enter the Monjasa fleet under the following names: • Monjasa Tracer – formerly Eva Schulte (2010) • Monjasa Tuner – formerly Erika Schulte (2011) • Monjasa Twister – formerly Everhard Schulte (2010) • Monjasa Tracker – formerly Edzard Schulte (2011) • Monjasa Trigger – formerly Elisabeth Schulte (2010) Following the acquisitions, Monjasa’s fleet comprises 20 owned tankers and around 10 vessels on time charter. articles.title: Korea and China vie to lead ammonia-fueled shipping market
articles.summary: Korean and Chinese shipbuilders are locked in a battle of pride over ships that carry ammonia. Korea is highlighting the world’s largest ammonia “propulsion ship,” while China is rolling out an ammonia “carrier.” The situation signals fierce competition for the next-generation ship market. articles.body: Korea and China vie to lead ammonia-fueled shipping market in Shipbuilding News 12/11/2026 Korean and Chinese shipbuilders are locked in a battle of pride over ships that carry ammonia. Korea is highlighting the world’s largest ammonia “propulsion ship,” while China is rolling out an ammonia “carrier.” The situation signals fierce competition for the next-generation ship market. According to the shipbuilding industry on the 3rd, HD Hyundai Heavy Industries said last month it built the “world’s largest” ammonia propulsion ship. It is an ultra-large ammonia propulsion ship with a 93,000 ㎥ cargo tank capacity ordered in 2023 by Singapore’s EPS (Eastern Pacific Shipping). An ammonia propulsion ship uses ammonia as engine fuel. Earlier in June, Jiangnan Shipyard under China’s largest shipbuilding group, China State Shipbuilding Corporation (CSSC), delivered to EPS an ultra-large ammonia carrier (VLAC; Very Large Ammonia Carrier) with the same cargo tank capacity as HD Hyundai Heavy Industries and described it as the “world’s largest” VLAC. Both ships carry ammonia, an eco-friendly fuel, but their propulsion systems differ. HD Hyundai Heavy Industries uses ammonia and bunker fuel as ship fuel, while Jiangnan Shipyard’s vessel uses liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) and bunker fuel. The view is that HD Hyundai Heavy Industries used the expression “world’s largest” ammonia propulsion ship to emphasize its differentiation in both carrying ammonia (carrier) and using it as propulsion fuel (propulsion ship). In the shipbuilding industry, the subtle sparring between the two builders is seen as another example of intensifying Korea–China competition in the high-value gas carrier market, where Korea had held an edge. A major Greek shipowner that had entrusted only Korean shipbuilders with gas carrier construction recently ordered a VLAC from a Chinese shipbuilder for the first time. Earlier, in April, HD Hyundai Heavy Industries completed construction of its first ammonia propulsion ship, the 46,000 ㎥ mid-size ammonia-fueled gas carrier Antwerpen, and delivered it in June to the owner (Exmar LPG France). At the time, HD Hyundai Heavy Industries said it “succeeded in building the world’s first ammonia propulsion ship.” A shipbuilding industry official said, “Commercializing a large 93,000 ㎥ vessel with ammonia fuel propulsion is meaningful,” and noted, “Even if both are 93,000 ㎥ ultra-large ammonia carriers, HD Hyundai Heavy Industries is differentiated in that it applied an ammonia propulsion system to a large ship.” Ammonia is drawing attention in the shipping and shipbuilding industries as a carbon-free, eco-friendly fuel that does not emit carbon dioxide. The International Energy Agency (IEA) projected the share of ammonia among marine fuels to rise from 8% in 2030 to 46% in 2050. However, because ammonia is toxic, corrosive, and has high density, safety technologies such as leak detection and emissions reduction and recovery are critical. This is why ammonia carriers and propulsion ships are classified as high-difficulty, high-value ship types compared with bulk carriers or tankers. Korea and China are engaged in fierce competition for leadership in the ammonia carrier and propulsion ship market. In new orders for ammonia carriers, China has begun to pull ahead. Of the 40 VLACs ordered worldwide from January to July this year, China won 26 (65%) and Korea won 14 (35%). In particular, China’s Hengli Heavy Industry Group won the most orders during this period, with 14 ships. Hengli Heavy Industry recently won orders for two 88,000 ㎥ VLACs from Alphagas under Greece’s Anna Angelicoussis shipping group. The reason this contract is drawing attention in the shipbuilding and shipping industries is that Alphagas chose a Chinese shipbuilder for the first time instead of a Korean one. Alphagas, which had mainly operated LNG carriers, entered the ultra-large ammonia carrier market in 2024 and entrusted construction to Hanwha Ocean and HD Hyundai Heavy Industries. Including vessels currently under construction, Alphagas’ fleet (16 ships) consists of 10 LNG carriers and 6 VLACs. Except for the two recently ordered from Hengli Heavy Industry, all were entrusted to Hanwha Ocean and HD Hyundai Heavy Industries. In China as well, construction of ammonia propulsion ships that use ammonia as ship fuel is increasing. After acquiring WinGD, a Swiss-based holder of original engine technology, it has also begun producing its own ammonia dual-fuel engines based on WinGD’s designs. CSSC acquired the two-stroke marine engine business of Finland’s Wärtsilä in 2014 and established the joint venture WinGD. It then acquired the remaining 30% equity from Wärtsilä in 2016 and now holds 100% equity. Yang Jong-seo, a professor in the department of naval architecture and ocean engineering at Seoul National University, said, “It is an enviable situation that China, after acquiring WinGD, is creating its own engine models and developing equipment together to grow the ecosystem.” Source: Chosunbiz 2026-11-12 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Smart Port Challenge 2026 Marks 10 Years of Growing Maritime Innovation in Port News 12/11/2026 The Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) and NUSX, the entrepreneurial heart of the National University of Singapore (NUS), announced the winners of the 10th PIER71 Smart Port Challenge (SPC) at its Grand Finale today. From AI and robotics innovation for ships, to port automation and maritime cybersecurity solutions, this year’s Challenge attracted a record 586 proposals from 281 start-ups across 39 countries (see Annex A), reflecting growing international interest in developing technology solutions for the maritime industry. Showcasing Maritime Innovation at SPC 2026 Ocean Intelligence from Australia won the Top Start-up Prize for its AI-powered voyage optimisation platform that incorporates ocean currents, weather conditions and vessel characteristics to identify more fuel-efficient routes. Vueron Technology from South Korea received the Top Scale-up Prize for its AI-powered LiDAR perception solutions for autonomous mobility and industrial safety. The prizes, at S$15,000 each, were sponsored by Columbia Group and Temasek respectively. Trunk Technology (Beijing) from China was also acknowledged by the Judges with a Special Mention. Four thematic prizes of S$10,000 each were also awarded: Underwater Solution from South Korea received the Digitalisation Prize, sponsored by RINA; Ocean Intelligence from Australia received the Maritime Green Technologies Prize, sponsored by OCBC; Trunk Technology (Beijing) from China received the Smart Port Prize, sponsored by PSA Singapore and PSA Ventures; and Vueron Technology from South Korea received the Smart Shipping Prize, sponsored by American Bureau of Shipping (ABS). Details of the winners are in Annex B. The finalists and semi-finalists also demonstrated the breadth of technologies being developed for maritime operations. Robotic systems that automate cargo hold cleaning and confined-space inspections reduce the need for personnel to enter hazardous environments. AI-powered cybersecurity platforms monitor onboard IT and operational technology networks in real time, detecting threats as they emerge. Biological sensor networks use molluscs as living sensors, giving ports early warning of oil leaks and toxic discharges. Together, these solutions point to exciting opportunities to make the maritime industry safer, greener and more secure. The full list of finalists and semi-finalists, their countries of origin and proposed solutions is in Annex C. From this year’s submissions, 21 start-ups from 11 countries were selected for the 10-week SPC Accelerate programme[1], with eight progressing to the Grand Finale. Participants worked on solutions addressing 20 innovation opportunities identified by maritime companies across digitalisation, maritime green technologies, next generation port and smart shipping. Letters of Intent were signed between participating start-ups and 28 maritime companies to explore proof-of-concept and pilot projects. Ten Years of Growing Maritime Innovation Since the first Smart Port Challenge in 2017, SPC has grown to a record 586 proposals from 281 start-ups across 39 countries this year. Over its 10 editions, the Challenge has attracted over 2,100 proposals and nurtured over 200 startups through the SPC Accelerate Programme bringing together technology companies and maritime industry partners to develop solutions for operational needs. PIER71 has also supported more than 200 start-ups since 2018, which have collectively raised S$180 million in capital. Among its alumni, BeeX, an SPC 2020 winner, completed a S$10 million fundraising round this year to expand its autonomous underwater vehicle operations internationally. CRecTech, an SPC 2023 runner-up, signed a technology agreement with Pertamina NRE in 2026 to supply catalyst technology for a pilot plant in Indonesia exploring bio-methanol production. Helping Maritime Start-ups Commercialise and Scale PIER71 is extending its support beyond the development and testing of solutions to help maritime start-ups access investors and overseas markets. As part of SPC 2026, two initiatives introduced in April — Venture2Capital[2] and Ascend[3] — provide additional opportunities for start-ups to secure investment connections and pursue overseas business development. Venture2Capital’s inaugural edition connected six SPC participating start-ups with 11 venture capital and corporate investors to present their solutions and discuss potential investment opportunities. Ascend’s inaugural cohort includes BeeCharge, which develops solar-powered mobile charging solutions supported by predictive energy management software. BeeCharge has begun engaging maritime industry contacts in Europe to explore potential business partnerships. PIER71 also expanded its international network this year through partnerships with Digital Hub Logistics & Commerce in Hamburg, PortXL in Rotterdam and Braid Theory in Los Angeles. These partnerships provide selected start-ups with access to overseas innovation programmes, industry networks and market-entry support in Europe and the United States. KinetixPro, an SPC 2024 alumnus whose computer vision platform uses existing CCTV infrastructure to monitor safety risks, is establishing Hamburg as a base for its European expansion through Digital Hub Logistics & Commerce’s network. The new agreements add to PIER71’s network of over 70 industry partners. PIER71 is also attracting international technology companies to establish a presence in Singapore. Through its Landing Pad programme[4], four start-ups from Belgium, Germany, China and India incorporated businesses in Singapore this year. The programme currently has 39 active members. Among them is Belgian drone logistics company ADLC, which obtained a Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore Unmanned Aircraft Operator Permit covering beyond-visual-line-of-sight operations and the carriage of dangerous goods. On 17 August 2026, ADLC subsequently demonstrated a 13-kilometre cargo drone route between the Maritime Drone Estate and Pulau Sebarok, illustrating the potential for drone deliveries to offshore maritime facilities. See Annex D for details on PIER71 international partnerships and other notable community activities in 2026. Mr Ang Wee Keong, Chief Executive of MPA, said, “Over the past decade, the Smart Port Challenge has brought technology start-ups and maritime companies together to develop solutions for industry needs. The range of technologies showcased this year reflects the opportunities for innovation across maritime operations. We will continue to help promising start-ups develop and commercialise their solutions, connect with investors and reach international markets, while attracting new capabilities and investments that strengthen Maritime Singapore.” Dr Tan Sian Wee, NUS Senior Vice President (Innovation and Enterprise), said, “Raising capital remains one of the hardest steps for deep tech founders. This is why PIER71 does more than nurture ideas. With the Smart Port Challenge and Venture2Capital, we are bringing start-ups closer to real deployment, which is what gives investors confidence. PIER71 start-ups have now collectively raised more than S$180 million, and we are building a clear pathway from pilot to scale for maritime innovators.” Mr Demetris Chrysostomou, Columbia Group Deputy Chief Executive Officer, said, “At Columbia Group, we believe in contributing to the wider maritime ecosystem by supporting initiatives that encourage innovation and entrepreneurship. The PIER71 Smart Port Challenge provides an important platform for emerging companies to develop their ideas alongside industry partners, and we are pleased to contribute our experience and support to this initiative.” Source: Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore 2026-11-12 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: International Container Terminal Services, Inc. reported double-digit growth in volumes, revenues and earnings for the first nine months of 2026. Consolidated volume reached 12,114,429 TEUs in the nine months, up 13% from 10,687,128 TEUs. Third-quarter throughput was 8% higher at 3,998,671 TEUs against 3,698,053 TEUs. Revenue from port operations rose 24% to US$ 2.90 billion from US$ 2.34 billion, and EBITDA rose 21% to US$ 1.87 billion from US$ 1.54 billion. Net income attributable to equity holders increased 20% to US$ 898.89 million from US$ 751.56 million, driven mainly by higher operating income. The increase came mainly from two new terminals: Durban Gateway Terminal, which took over port operations of DCT Pier 2 in South Africa in January 2026, and Batu Ampar Container Terminal in Batam, Indonesia, which began operating in September 2025. Improved trade in Asia and the Americas also helped, partly offset by lower volumes at certain EMEA terminals, mainly Basra Gateway Terminal in Iraq because of the Middle East conflict, and by the deconsolidation of Yantai. Excluding the new and discontinued operations, volume would have edged up 0.1%. Revenue growth reflected higher volumes with a favourable container mix, more ancillary services, tariff adjustments at certain terminals, contributions from Durban and Batam, and favourable currency translation from the Mexican peso, Australian dollar and Brazilian real. These were partly offset by the Basra decline, the Yantai deconsolidation and the weaker Philippine peso. Excluding new and discontinued operations, revenue would have grown 15%. EBITDA margin declined to 64 percent from 66 percent because of the integration of newly acquired operations; excluding them, EBITDA would have grown 15% and the margin would have improved slightly to above 66%. Chairman and President Enrique K. Razon Jr. said the diversified portfolio provides resilience in a more challenging operating environment, that the focus remains on integrating new terminals and investing in capacity and service levels, and that disciplined capital allocation and operational execution remain central to delivering sustainable shareholder value.

articles.body: Business & Finance November 12, 2026 · 6 minutes ago With restructuring done, Impact Oil & Gas turns into pure-play Namibia explorer The corporate restructuring has established a pure-play Namibia-focused development and exploration business, anchored by the Venus project. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Illustration Source: Meren Canada’s Meren Energy has cleared the final regulatory hurdle to streamline its portfolio, announcing the completion of a major corporate restructuring for its investee company, which transforms Impact Oil & Gas into a focused, lower-cost, pure-play exploration and development business anchored in Namibia, retaining the Canadian firm’s stake in the Venus light oil discovery while relieving it of the costs associated with non-core South African assets. The completion of the corporate restructuring, which was first announced on May 26, 2026, follows receipt of the required South African regulatory approvals and joint venture partner consents, enabling Impact to become a pure-play Namibia-focused explorer and marking a further step in Meren’s strategy to simplify its business and high-grade its portfolio around its core areas of value creation in the Orange Basin. The Canadian player’s effective interest in its core Namibian assets, including the Venus project, is unchanged, while Impact’s South African exploration interests, which were non-core to Meren, have now been separated out, concentrating on the firm’s Orange Basin exposure alongside its direct carried interest in Block 3B/4B, offshore South Africa, which is unaffected by the transaction. Impact has completed the sale of its entire shareholding in Impact Africa, the subsidiary that holds its South African exploration licenses, together with certain related assets, to Impact Energies, formerly IOG Energies, a wholly owned subsidiary of Deepkloof, which is the investee company's majority shareholder. The firm's primary assets are now its 9.5% undivided participating interest in blocks 2912 and 2913B, offshore Namibia, which contain the Venus light oil discovery operated by TotalEnergies. The company's approximate 20% shareholding in Africa Energy Corp. was not part of the transaction and has been retained. With the intention of making a clear distinction from Impact Energies, Meren’s Impact intends to change its corporate name in due course, which will have no effect on its business, assets, or shareholdings. The restructuring is intended to simplify the firm’s portfolio and allow it to concentrate on its interests in Namibia, where the TotalEnergies-operated joint venture is working towards a final investment decision (FID) on the Venus development. Meren, which will no longer bear the costs of managing and maintaining the divested South African exploration assets, expects this more focused structure to support clearer capital allocation going forward. " Completing the Impact restructuring delivers another milestone in the portfolio program we have been executing since late 2023. Through Impact, Meren’s effective interest in Venus is unchanged, and Impact is now a simpler, lower-cost vehicle centered on Namibia. Together with our direct interest in Block 3B/4B, this strengthens Meren’s long-term position in the Orange Basin. I would like to thank Impact’s management team and our fellow shareholders in Impact for their work in bringing the transaction to completion. articles.body: Americas Dry Cargo Brazilian soybean exports smash records Sam Chambers November 12, 2026 0 299 1 minute read Norden Norden Brazilian soybean exports have smashed all previous records, with shipments during the first ten months of 2026 already exceeding the whole of last year’s total, providing a significant boost to dry bulk shipping demand, primarily panamaxes and supramaxes. New analysis from Ursa Shipbrokers shows seaborne soybean exports reached 108.4m tonnes between January and October, an increase of 7.9%, or 7.9m tonnes, compared with the same period last year. The ten-month total was also 600,000 tonnes higher than shipments during the whole of 2025. The second quarter proved particularly strong, with exports climbing 10.3% to 44.9m tonnes, while third-quarter volumes increased 8.1% to 29.7m tonnes. October shipments reached 6.5m tonnes, up 2.4% year-on-year, although volumes declined almost 14% from September as the previous harvest season wound down. Brazilian government customs data independently confirms the record-breaking trend, although its figures differ slightly from Ursa’s vessel-tracking estimates. Official exports reached 106.5m tonnes through October, up 5.9% year-on-year, generating $46bn in export revenue. The outlook suggests further records could follow. The US Department of Agriculture’s latest forecasts put Brazil’s 2026/27 soybean harvest at 186m tonnes, with exports projected to reach 118m tonnes. The growth is being driven primarily by increased acreage rather than higher yields, with harvested area forecast to expand to 50m hectares. Brazil’s own crop agency, Conab, is more conservative, projecting production of approximately 181.6m tonnes. With China remaining the dominant destination for Brazilian soybeans, further export growth has the potential to support tonne-mile demand well into 2027, something that will be under the microscope when the Agri-Commodities panel reconvenes on April 28 at Geneva Dry , the world’s premier commodities shipping conference. articles.title: HMM operating profit surges 370% in third quarter

articles.body: South Korean container shipping company HMM reported a sharp increase in earnings for the third quarter of 2026, with operating profit rising 370% year-on-year amid improvements in operational efficiency and profitability across its shipping businesses. The carrier recorded consolidated revenue of KRW 4.13 trillion during the quarter, up 52% from KRW 2.71 trillion in the corresponding period of 2025. Operating profit climbed to KRW 1.40 trillion from KRW 297 billion a year earlier, while net profit increased 405% to KRW 1.54 trillion, compared with KRW 304 billion in the third quarter of 2025. The company reported an operating profit margin of approximately 34%, reflecting its ongoing focus on cost optimisation and efficient fleet operations. Compared with the second quarter of 2026, revenue increased by 21%, while operating profit rose by 294% and net profit advanced by 273%. Container division strengthens nine-month earnings HMM’s container shipping division recorded operating profit of KRW 1.64 trillion during the first nine months of 2026, representing a 55.3% increase compared with the same period last year. According to the company, the division focused on expanding its shipping network and securing higher-yield cargo through its hub-and-spoke strategy. HMM said these operational measures supported profitability despite continued global uncertainty, including geopolitical risks in the Middle East and natural disasters affecting major ports. Across the Group, revenue for the first nine months reached KRW 10.25 trillion, an increase of 25% from KRW 8.18 trillion in the corresponding period of 2025. Cumulative operating profit rose 76% to KRW 2.02 trillion, compared with KRW 1.14 trillion a year earlier, while net profit increased 52% to KRW 2.30 trillion. Bulk shipping growth supports diversification HMM’s bulk shipping division also delivered stronger results during the nine-month period, with operating profit increasing 418.5% year-on-year to KRW 378 billion. The segment’s contribution to total operating profit rose from 6.4% to 18.8%, reflecting the growing importance of the company’s non-container shipping activities. HMM attributed the bulk division’s performance to its long-term contracts, which helped maintain a stable revenue base amid market volatility. The company is also continuing to diversify its fleet beyond dry bulk carriers and tankers, expanding into pure car and truck carriers (PCTCs), gas carriers and multipurpose vessels (MPVs). The latest results highlight HMM’s improved earnings performance across both its container and bulk shipping businesses, with the container division remaining the largest contributor to operating profit.

articles.title: Why shipowners might be better off sharing profits than taking on debt
articles.summary: Traditional loans demand repayments regardless of freight markets. articles.body: Contributions Finance and Insurance Why shipowners might be better off sharing profits than taking on debt Splash November 12, 2026 0 219 3 minutes read Traditional loans demand repayments regardless of freight markets. Earnings-sharing structures offer a different proposition: investors participate in a vessel’s fortunes while owners retain control. Captain Vikas Pandey from Shipfinex explains. Ship finance looks healthy on paper. Petrofin Research estimates that the top 40 shipping banks grew their portfolios by 6% in 2025 to $300.6bn, and puts total ship finance across banks, leasing, export credit and alternative lenders at around $680bn. Societe Generale expects 2026 to remain a borrower’s market, with top-tier owners seeing margins of 100 to 150 basis points over SOFR. That is accurate for owners at the top. It is less accurate for the rest. Petrofin’s index of global bank ship finance stands at 63 against 100 in 2008, while the value of the fleet and orderbook has risen to about $2.17trn. Small and mid-sized owners, who by one industry estimate own up to 60% of the world’s ships, still meet low advance ratios on older tonnage, higher margins, or alternative lenders asking for equity kickers and profit participation on top of interest. For these owners, a third structure is worth understanding: selling a share of a single vessel’s future net earnings to outside investors, while the owner keeps title, management and commercial control. Cost. Where an owner can borrow at today’s bank margins, debt is almost always cheaper. Investors taking freight-market risk expect returns closer to equity. The comparison changes when the realistic alternative is private credit priced well above bank debt, with fees, tighter covenants and a profit share attached. At that point the owner is already paying for equity risk while still carrying the rigidity of a loan. Cash flow. This is the bigger difference. Debt service is fixed. Amortisation often runs shorter than the vessel’s remaining economic life, a balloon creates refinancing risk at maturity, and a minimum value clause can force prepayment or extra security when asset values fall. None of this adjusts when the charter market softens. An earnings share does. Investors receive an agreed percentage of net operating cash flow, so distributions fall when rates fall, and a weak quarter is not a default event. For an owner whose main exposure is a liquidity squeeze in a downturn, rather than the headline cost of capital, that flexibility has real value. Control. Investors in an earnings-share structure hold an economic right, not title. The vessel typically sits in a single-ship SPV that remains the registered owner, and the owner keeps technical and commercial management, crewing and chartering. Investors receive regular reporting and a vote on a short list of reserved matters, such as a sale of the vessel, new borrowing or a change of manager. A lender’s covenants, by contrast, can restrict distributions, require consent for employment and accelerate the loan on breach. Both structures constrain the owner, in different places. When it fits. Earnings-sharing tends to make sense where bank debt is unavailable or priced close to equity; where the vessel has visible employment, such as a period charter, that investors can underwrite; where the owner needs to protect liquidity through the cycle; or where equity is locked in an unencumbered vessel that the owner wants to release without selling. For an owner with cheap bank finance and a firm view that rates will rise, it gives away upside. Before signing, owners should settle the definition of net earnings and deductible costs, the treatment of off-hire and drydocking, reserve funding, the term and any cap on investor returns, buy-back rights, and what happens on a sale or total loss. Where a first-priority registered ship mortgage is in place, the mortgagee’s consent is required and investor distributions rank behind debt service. Debt remains the cheapest capital in shipping for owners who can get it on good terms. For many who cannot, sharing earnings matches the cost of capital to the way a ship actually earns its money. articles.summary: Danish shipping giant AP Moller-Maersk has confirmed another cybersecurity breach after hackers gained access to an older IT system and extracted data, nearly a decade after the devastating NotPetya attack that cost the company up to $300m. articles.body: Containers Europe Maersk hit by fresh cyber breach Adis Ajdin November 12, 2026 0 2,173 1 minute read Cydome Cydome Danish shipping giant AP Moller-Maersk has confirmed another cybersecurity breach after hackers gained access to an older IT system and extracted data, nearly a decade after the devastating NotPetya attack that cost the company up to $300m. The Copenhagen-headquartered group said on Wednesday that the incident involved a local legacy system inherited through a previous acquisition. Maersk’s cybersecurity team launched an investigation after discovering the intrusion and has taken steps to secure the affected system.”Our findings so far strongly suggest no sensitive data has been disclosed,” the company said. The carrier said the breach appeared to be confined to the legacy system, with no indication that other Maersk systems or those belonging to customers and partners connected through APIs and electronic data interchange (EDI) had been compromised. The company added that it does not expect disruption to customer operations, with its digital booking and shipment management platforms continuing to operate normally. Maersk has not identified the acquired business involved, disclosed what data was extracted or named those responsible for the intrusion. The announcement follows separate claims by a hacker group calling itself WhiteArmor that it had obtained around 100 GB of logistics data from a platform associated with LF Logistics, the Hong Kong-based logistics business Maersk acquired for $3.6bn in 2022. The group has reportedly demanded $5m in bitcoin. The claims remain unverified, and Maersk has not confirmed any connection between the alleged theft and the incident it is investigating. The latest breach brings back memories of June 2017, when the NotPetya malware attack crippled Maersk’s IT infrastructure and disrupted container shipping and terminal operations worldwide. The Danish group subsequently put the financial damage at between $250m and $300m, making it one of the costliest cyber incidents in shipping history.
